composition: Nominal composition of the alloy is Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%). The chemistry measured by EDS is Fe 41.6, Mn 34.8, Al 18.6, Cu 5.0 at.% (Table 1); the table also shows that across the 15Al → 17Al → 19Al series the Al increase is achieved by substituting Al for Fe, with Mn (≈35 at.%) and Cu (≈5 at.%) held essentially constant. The high Mn level (≈35 at.%) was chosen to promote the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase; Al is the primary density-reducing element (each 1 wt.% Al lowers density by roughly 0.1 g/cm³) and also influences β-Mn precipitation; Cu was previously shown to accelerate the aging-hardening response and raise the hardness of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel.
conclusions: The 19Al solution-treated sample is the soft, single-phase α (BCC) baseline of a study demonstrating that Fe-35Mn-(15, 17, 19)Al-5Cu (at.%) low-density steels can be tuned to an ultra-wide, flexible hardness window of 253.4–965.6 HV by simple aging treatments, driven by the continuous precipitation of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase. Relative to the other two alloys, higher Al content (i) lowers density (6.66 g/cm³ for 19Al), (ii) raises solution-treated hardness modestly through solid-solution strengthening, but (iii) slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn (in the 19Al alloy the α → β-Mn transformation requires about 10 h at 550 °C versus 6 h for 17Al and 3 h at 525 °C for 15Al), and (iv) lowers the peak hardness (917.8 HV for 19Al vs 924.9 HV for 17Al and 965.6 HV for 15Al) and the fracture toughness of the hardest state (3.5 MPa·m^1/2 for 19Al vs 6.6 and 8.6 MPa·m^1/2). The work's practical significance is that these alloys can be shaped in the soft solution-treated state and then aged to a chosen hardness level ("one material, multiple uses"), and that the parent Fe-35.2Mn-15Al-5.2Cu alloy reaches an ultra-high specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g; the trade-off between hardness and toughness, however, still requires optimization.
mechanisms: Increasing the Al content from 15 to 19 at.% raises the amount of Al in solid solution in the α (BCC) matrix, so the solution-treated hardness increases with Al content through solid-solution strengthening; the 19Al alloy therefore shows the highest solution-treated hardness of the series (263.8 ± 1.1 HV vs 259.8 HV for 17Al and 253.4 HV for 15Al).

Raising Al from 15 to 19 at.% markedly refines the grain structure of the solution-treated alloy, as seen in the EBSD inverse-pole-figure maps, so higher Al produces a finer, equiaxed α grain structure.

The solution-treated state is a single-phase α (BCC) solid solution that acts as the parent phase for aging: during subsequent aging the α matrix transforms to the Mn-rich, ultra-hard β-Mn phase, and the near-complete α → β-Mn transformation is the microstructural origin of the alloy's ultra-high hardness.

Because β-Mn is an Mn-rich phase, its nucleation and growth require long-range atomic diffusion that excludes Fe, Al and Cu to the surroundings; an increase in Al content enriches more Al around β-Mn and stabilizes the Al-rich D0₃ phase (whose precipitation and growth must be depleted before β-Mn can form), both of which hinder β-Mn nucleation and growth and slow its precipitation kinetics, lengthening the time needed for the α → β-Mn transformation in the higher-Al alloys.

Increasing the aging temperature accelerates β-Mn precipitation by raising both the driving force for β-Mn formation and the atomic diffusion rate, which is why the 19Al alloy's optimal ultra-high-hardness window shifts to higher temperature (575–625 °C) than that of the lower-Al alloys.
microstructure: The solution-treated 19Al alloy is a single-phase α solid solution with a body-centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. EBSD phase maps of the solution-treated 15Al, 17Al and 19Al alloys are uniformly red, corresponding to α (BCC), and no γ (FCC) region is resolved in any of them. The inverse-pole-figure map of the solution-treated 19Al alloy reveals a fine, equiaxed, multi-coloured grain structure; comparing the three solution-treated alloys shows that raising Al from 15 to 19 at.% markedly refines the grain structure (the 19Al map is much finer and more equiaxed than the coarse-grained 15Al and 17Al maps). No quantitative grain size, phase fraction or texture values, and no precipitates or defects, are reported for this state — it is confirmed as a precipitate-free single-phase α matrix that acts as the starting point for the later α → β-Mn transformation, in which β-Mn precipitates preferentially along α grain boundaries and within α grains.
processing: The alloy was produced by vacuum induction furnace melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere into an ingot of nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%). The ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h and then hot-rolled into 4 mm-thick plates. Plates were cut by electrical discharge machining into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens for Vickers hardness testing and microstructural characterization. The defining step for this sample is the solution treatment: 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching, which sets the soft, single-phase α (BCC) solid-solution state. Specimens for Vickers hardness, XRD, SEM and EBSD were then prepared by electrolytic polishing in a mixture of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol. This sample is the parent state of the study's aging schedule (subsequent aging at 525–650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h with water quenching).
properties: Vickers microhardness of the solution-treated 19Al alloy is 263.8 ± 1.1 HV (load 9.8 N for 15 s; average of 5 measurements per sample). It is the highest of the three alloys' solution-treated values, and the solution-treated hardness was found to increase with rising Al content, attributed to solid-solution strengthening. Density, measured by the Archimedes method at ambient temperature, is 6.66 g/cm³ (compared with 6.85 g/cm³ for 15Al and 6.76 g/cm³ for 17Al), the lowest of the series. This solution-treated condition is the soft end of the study's overall hardness window (253.4–965.6 HV across all alloys and aging conditions). Characterization techniques applied to this sample and its alloy family include Vickers microhardness testing (HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester), EBSD (GeminiSEM 300 SEM, step sizes 1.5 µm and 0.05 µm), SEM/EDS (ZEISS Sigma 300 at 5 kV; FEI Talos F200X TEM with EDS at 200 kV), XRD (D8 Discover), Archimedes density measurement, and nanoindentation (Agilent G200).
summary: The "19Al solution-treated" sample is the soft, solid-solution state of the Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) low-density steel examined in a study of how Al content governs the aging-hardening behaviour of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels. It consists of a single-phase α (BCC) solid solution obtained by solution treating a homogenized and hot-rolled plate at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon followed by oil quenching. This state is the common baseline (263.8 ± 1.1 HV) from which every aging treatment in the study proceeds and provides the context for the paper's core question: how increasing Al content (15 → 19 at.%) affects the precipitation kinetics of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase and the resulting hardness, specific hardness and fracture toughness.
unmapped: Elastic modulus of the 19Al alloy is 181 GPa, measured through compressive stress-strain curves (alongside 164 GPa for 15Al and 175 GPa for 17Al); the paper does not state which heat-treatment state this value corresponds to. It is used only in Eq. (1) for the fracture-toughness evaluation of the peak-hardness samples, so it is not a property of the solution-treated state specifically.

EDS-measured composition of the 19Al alloy (at.%) from Table 1 is Fe 41.6, Mn 34.8, Al 18.6, Cu 5.0; this is the alloy chemistry of the examined solution-treated sample, differing slightly from the nominal Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu.
